messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stays a half-step behind Bram's shoulder and does not look at the man in the doorway for long. He looks at the yard instead: the hammers lying in the dust, the half-loaded cart with its traces hanging loose, the open shed doors, the spoil heaps with no one picking through them.

"Nobody's working this place," he says quietly, not moving his lips much. "Tools dropped, not put away. Somebody left in a hurry, or somebody made them leave." He lets his eyes travel back to the house and the man's folded arms. "Keep your hands where he can see them. I want to see what's behind him before I decide he's just a warden."

He takes one step to the left, toward the edge of the lower cut where a fallen wagon wheel gives some cover, and waits to see whether the man moves.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram stops at the edge of the yard and lets the others come up on his flanks. He doesn't take his eyes off the doorway.

"Hold here a moment, Pell, Sefa." Quietly, to the two of them: "Pell, go wide to the left, keep behind the spoil heap, and tell me if anything moves up on the terraces. Sefa, stay with me and keep your hands where he can see them."

He sets his shield a little higher and walks forward three slow paces, far enough to be heard across the yard but not so far that he's in the doorway's reach.

"Warden! Maela Thorn, the apothecary in Beregost, sent us. We're for the sealed case of dye-salts, the one that's to go to her shop by sunset." He lifts his empty hand and nods at the half-loaded cart, the scattered tools. "Where's your crew? Nothing's worked here since the bell, by the look of it. Is everyone all right?"

He keeps his longsword in its scabbard, but his eyes go to the ring of keys, then to the shadow inside the house, then back to the man's folded arms, reading whether he is waiting for a greeting or for something else.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa stops at the edge of the yard, a step ahead of the others, and lets her eyes go over the scene before she speaks. The abandoned hammers, the half-loaded cart with no mule, the single thread of smoke. Her hand settles on the prayer beads at her throat.

"Good morning to you," she calls, pitching her voice to carry without shouting. "We're from Maela Thorn's shop in Beregost. We've come for the sealed case she arranged with the warden here. My name is Sefa Marrin; these are my companions, Pell and Bram." She lets a small, easy smile reach her face. "Is the warden inside? We have until sunset to get the case back to Beregost, and I'd rather not spend the afternoon standing in the dust."

Under her breath, without turning her head, she says to the others: "Keep your hands where he can see them. Something emptied this place in a hurry, and I'd like to know what before we go near that door."

scenes.narration:
Osric does not come down the step. He watches Bram's shoulder, then Sefa's hands, then the wagon wheel where Pell has gone to ground, and only then does he unfold his arms.

"Maela's," he says. It is not a question. His voice is dry from the dust, and he takes his time with each word.

Pell reaches the wheel without a sound. From there the yard lies open: the lifting frame bare of its rope, the shed doors standing wide, the spoil heaps with nobody picking through them. Behind the house, where the cut narrows, a line of boot-prints runs down toward the track, and a second line of hoofprints cuts beside it, stopping and starting. The mule is gone and so is the crew.

Bram reads the ground as he would a road he has walked for ten years. The cart's ruts end where the traces were cut loose; the hoofprints head east along the track toward Beregost, deep where a loaded beast was pushed. Two days old, at least, and no one came back for the cart. He says nothing about it yet, only shifts his shield and keeps his eyes on the doorway.

"Ninety was Maela's price," Osric says. "Dye-salts, sealed, to her buyer." He turns his head toward the cart, then back. "It's a hundred and sixty now. Gold. On the step, before the lid comes off." He does not smile. "Or the case stays on the shelf, and you walk back down the track with your cart empty."

Behind him, in the dark of the house, something on a shelf catches a little light and then goes dull again. He does not look round at it.

"Crew's gone," he adds, as if it were the same business. "Don't ask me where."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram keeps his shield up and does not move closer to the doorway. He speaks evenly, loud enough for Pell and Sefa to hear.

"Ninety, Osric. That's what Maela agreed with us, and it's to be paid on delivery, not on the step." He tips his head toward the track behind them. "I've walked this road ten years. Your cart's been standing two days, not since the bell this morning. So you're telling me the crew left two days back, and somebody's been asking you for more money since. Who?"

He lets the question sit, watching Osric's face and the hand that has not left the doorframe.

"I'm not paying a hundred and sixty out of my own purse, and I'm not carrying an argument back to Maela's shop. Show me the case. Let me see the seal. If it's what she bought, she'll pay the ninety in her own shop, and I'll stand for it. If it isn't, we'll all go back and tell her so."

He glances once, quickly, toward the shelf in the dark, then back to Osric.

Quietly, out of the side of his mouth, to Sefa: "Watch the shelf, not his hands. And if he goes for the door, you get behind the wheel with Pell."

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa keeps her hands loose and open at her sides and does not move closer to the step. She looks at Osric for a long moment, then at the cart with its cut traces, then back at his face.

"A hundred and sixty is a strange price for dye-salts that were agreed at ninety yesterday," she says evenly. "Maela doesn't haggle with her own buyers, and she doesn't send us out at dawn to be cheated at the door. So I'd like to understand what's changed since then. Has someone else been asking for this case?"

She lets her gaze drift past him to the dark doorway, just long enough to mark the shelf and the faint glint on it, then returns to his eyes.

"And the crew. You say they've gone, and you don't know where. Did they leave on their own feet, or did someone make them leave?" Her voice softens, though it does not lose its edge. "I'm not here to take anything from you, Master Osric. Whatever happened in this yard, I'd rather know it before I'm standing in the middle of it."

Under her breath, to Bram and Pell: "He's frightened, and not of us. Watch the door."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell keeps his cheek against the cold iron rim of the wheel and lets his eyes go past Osric to the back of the house, where the cut narrows and the tracks run.

"A hundred and sixty," he says under his breath, loud enough for Bram to hear and no louder. "Maela said ninety, and ninety was already a fair price for walking out here. Ask him what happened to the crew before you ask him for anything. A man who won't say where his mule went is a man who may know where somebody else went too."

He stays low and studies the ground behind the house. The boot-prints run down toward the track, and he wants to know whether they were walked or dragged, and how many went out with their feet dug in.

presses.text:
Pell reads the dust the way he reads a ledger: from the bottom line up, looking for where the figures stop agreeing with themselves.

The boot-prints come down out of the cut in a loose line, and most of them are walked, heel-first, the stride long and easy. But three sets, close together near the back corner of the house, dig deep at the toe and skid. Someone was being pulled, or pushed hard, and was not going willingly. Beside those marks the hoofprints stop and start, and one of them has a shoe that is badly set. A mule that was led off in a hurry, not ridden.

He does not say any of it aloud yet. He keeps his voice to Bram and Sefa, low and flat.

"Two of them walked. Three were dragged, and the dragging starts at the back of the house, not the yard." He shifts his weight so the wheel's shadow stays over him. "Osric's still telling us they went on their own feet. Some of them didn't."

He lifts his eyes to the doorway, then past it to the shelf in the dark, where the thing caught the light.

"Bram, don't pay him a copper until you've seen the seal. Sefa, when he says 'the coin on the step,' ask him to show you the wax first, and keep your eyes on the shelf while he does." He pauses. "I'm going round the back of the house. If the tracks go in there, I want to know which door they used before anyone walks through the front."

He begins to move, low and quiet, toward the corner of the house, keeping the cart between himself and the step.

presses.text:
The marks give up their story easily once you know how to read them. Three sets of heels, dug in and skidding, run from the back corner of the house to a low plank door in the rear wall, and the door stands a finger's width open on a dark stair. Whoever was dragged went down that way, not out through the yard. A fresh boot-print sits on the top step, turned toward the house, not the track. Someone went back in that door after the others were taken, and it was not a man in a hurry.

The shadow on the lintel is wet, and the wax-smell of a fresh-broken seal hangs faintly in the air by the step. Somebody has been in the back of this house this morning, and they did not leave by the front.

Through the open gap, Pell hears a short scrape from below, then nothing.

Osric's voice carries round the corner from the front. "Have you found what you were looking for, or are you going to stand there till the sun goes down?"

Pell can stay at the back door and listen, slip down the stair in silence, or go back round to the wheel and tell Bram and Sefa what he has found before anyone moves.

presses.text:
The stone holds. Pell reaches the foot of the stair without a creak and stops in the mouth of a low cellar, pressed to the cold wall.

A lamp burns on a hook at the far end, turned low. Under it, a quarryman in dust-grey leathers sits against a timber post with his wrists bound behind him and a rag tied across his mouth. His eyes find Pell's shape in the stairwell before anything else moves. He does not make a sound, but his head jerks once toward the far corner.

There a stranger kneels among stacked crates in a dark travelling cloak with the hood up. He has already pried the lid off one crate, and the straw inside is pushed aside. A flat case of pale wood lies open on the floor beside him, its seal broken and its lid thrown back. He is turning something over in his gloved fingers, a small glass vial, holding it up to the lamp to see the colour. He has not looked toward the stair.

Something else lies at the edge of the lamplight: a second case, still sealed, with a seal of red wax and a thumb-print pressed into it. Beside it, on the flagstones, the dust is smeared with the drag of heels.

The stranger murmurs to himself, the words too low to carry, and reaches for the next crate.

Pell can move now, while the man's back is turned, and he has the shortsword and two daggers and the advantage of the stair behind him. He can wait and watch what the stranger does with the vial. He can go to the bound quarryman first and cut him loose. Or he can call up the stairs to Bram and bring the whole yard down into the cellar.

Sefa moves before Osric can settle his mind. She crosses the yard in four unhurried steps and stops at the corner of the house, placing herself between Osric and the plank door, close enough that he has to look at her to see past her.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram doesn't follow Osric's eyes to the back corner. He takes two long steps across the yard, placing himself between the old warden and the plank door, shield angled so it covers Osric's line of sight to the corner. He keeps his sword in its scabbard.

Bram looks at the keys in Osric's fist, then back at his face.

presses.text:
Pell hears it under the drip: a slow breath, drawn and let out through the teeth, the way a man breathes when he is working at something with his hands. Cloth whispers against stone. Two sounds, not one, and the second is lighter, a person standing still.

He leans out a finger's width past the bend. The white light comes from a shallow basin cut into the floor, where the seep pools over something pale that shines like ice. In its glow a dark-cloaked figure kneels with his back half to the passage, sliding a small glass vial into a fold of his sleeve. Beyond him, at the edge of the light, the quarryman's boots are visible on the flagstones, and a second pair stands behind a stacked pile of crates. Those boots do not move. Whoever wears them is watching the stair.

The kneeling man is not hurrying. He glances once at the basin, then closes his gloved hand around a second vial, and murmurs something that sounds like a prayer said backwards.

Pell has the advantage of the bend and the dark. The man at the crates has not seen him. The kneeling man has not turned. Nobody has yet called out.

Pell holds still against the wall and reads the dark around the bend, counting the drip and the faint hum of the seep.

Behind the drip, Pell hears the water move over stone, a slow wash and a small knock where a flake of chalk has come loose and settled into the channel. Under that there is nothing with breath in it: no cloth shifting, no weight on the wet floor, no boot. Whatever made the scrape was not standing and waiting at the turn.

The light is steady and cold, and it comes around the bend from low down, without flicker. Pell can hear, under the seep, a thin air-draught moving through a gap ahead, the kind of sound a shut room makes when someone has just opened its door a finger's width. Nothing answers when he breathes out.

The cellar is open to him now. He can lean out and look, or stay with his back to the wall and wait for the sound to come again.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram lowers his shield an inch, enough that Osric can see his face, and does not step back from the door.

"A letter for Maela. Then fetch it out and let her read it, and let me see the seal on the case while you're at it. A letter doesn't need a coin on the step."

He looks at the keys in Osric's fist, then at the hand flat against the doorframe.

"Here's my offer, and it's the only one I'm making. Ninety is what Maela agreed, and she pays it on delivery. I'll carry the case to her shop with my own hands. If the hundred and sixty is what your buyer wants, you take that up with Maela, not with three hired people on a road. You'll know by sunset whether she'll pay it, and so will I."

He drops his voice.

"Two men dragged something out of your cut. Somebody came up to your back door after your crew had gone. You're frightened of that corner, Osric, and you're frightened of whoever's been pricing your case for you. I can't stand guard on your house all day. But I'll stand between you and that corner for as long as you're honest with me. What's in that cut?"

Without turning, he calls low over his shoulder toward the wall: "Pell. Talk to me. Is there anybody inside but the warden?"

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa lets out a slow breath and lowers her hands an inch, slowly, so he can see every finger.

"A hundred and sixty is more than my purse holds, Master Osric, and I won't pretend otherwise. But I have eighteen gold in coin, and I'll put all of it on your step now, against Maela's name, as earnest. You'll have something in your hand before the rest is settled, and I'll write Maela's promise on the back of the receipt in my own hand."

She nods toward the threshold, not the door. "And the letter. Is it sealed, or is it open for Maela to read? If it's open, let me read it here, aloud, where Bram can hear it. I read a clerk's hand as easily as a healer's, and I'll tell you honestly what it says. If it says what you think, you'll know nobody is cheating you, and you won't have to stand on that step deciding alone."

Her eyes stay on his face. When his gaze flickers toward the corner of the house, she says his name once, quietly, and waits.

Under her breath, to Bram: "Don't let him close that door on the rest of the letter."

scenes.narration:
Bram lowers his shield the last inch, enough that Osric can see his face over the rim, and he does not give up the ground between the man and the corner.

"A letter doesn't need a coin on the step," he says. "Bring it out, let Maela read it, and let me look at the seal on the case while you do. That's a fair start."

He keeps the terms flat. Ninety on delivery, at Maela's shop, and he carries the case there with his own hands. Whatever the buyer pays above that is for Osric and Maela to settle, not three hired people on a road.

"You're frightened of that corner," he says, quieter. "You're frightened of whoever's been pricing your case for you. I can't stand guard on your house all day. I'll stand between you and that step for as long as you're straight with me. What came out of the cut?"

Sefa lowers her hands slowly, fingers spread so he can count them, then crouches and sets eight gold pieces and a platinum piece on the threshold stone. The coins sit bright against the grey chalk.

"Earnest," she says. "Against Maela's name. I'll write her promise on the receipt in my own hand."

Osric looks at the coins for a long moment. He does not reach for them.

"Eighteen on my step is eighteen on my step. The price is a hundred and sixty." He shifts his weight back onto the sill. "Leave it where it lies. It doesn't go in my pocket until the rest does."

"And the letter?" Sefa asks. "Is it sealed, or open for Maela to read?"

"Sealed. Same wax as the case." His hand stays flat against the doorframe. "It's for Maela. She reads it first, and you don't."

"What does it say?"

He is silent long enough that the seep drips somewhere under the yard. "It says I'm finished at Whitestone."

Bram's eyes stay on his face. When Osric's gaze slides once toward the back corner, Bram doesn't turn to follow it.

"The cut," Bram says.

"Stone." Osric's jaw works. "Walls cut before there was a Beregost. A door nobody can open, and water that goes white when it's dark. The men who cut it are in Beregost, drinking on it. Ask them, if you want the rest. Don't ask me."

He comes down one more step off the threshold, into the yard, and stops there with the keys in his fist. Behind him the shelf in the dark gives back its dull glint, and he still does not look round at it.

"Stand where you like," he says to Bram. "Not at my back door. Which of you wants the case, and which of you wants to see what's in my cut?"

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell doesn't trust the silence, but he doesn't waste a breath on it either. He stays low, shortsword sheathed, and eases his head round the bend just far enough to see the basin and the light coming off it. He keeps his hand on the wall and his weight on the balls of his feet, ready to pull back the moment anything turns toward him.

"Water and chalk, no boots," he breathes, pitched for the stair and no further. "Whatever knocked that stone went through the gap ahead. I'm going to look at the light before I walk into it."

He watches the basin's edge and the dark beyond the gap for any sign of a cloak or a hand, and waits for the draught to shift before he moves.

scenes.narration:
Pell eases his head past the bend, one finger's width at a time, and the cold light comes up to meet him. It has no lamp behind it. It rises off the seep water, which has pooled in a shallow cut in the floor and lies perfectly still, pale as frost under a moon that isn't there.

The cellar opens beyond the basin. On the left, the rock has been broken through at head height: a ragged hole a man's width across, stones heaped at its foot and half sunk in the water. Dust-white chalk slides down the broken edge in a fine trickle. Through the gap Pell sees a dark room, and on its far wall a stone face cut smooth and deliberately. A sunburst, its rays ending in small flames, all of them circling a hollow where something should sit. The hollow is empty.

Nothing moves in the water. The draught comes through the breach, cool and dry, and smells of cut stone and nothing living. Near the basin's edge a pick lies half-buried in the silt, its handle silvered with the same crust that coats the basin's rim. Beside it, two sets of boot-prints go down into the water's edge and come back out, and a third set goes down but does not come back.

The light holds steady. Nothing in the gap has shifted since Pell first looked, and the breath of the draught has not changed its rhythm.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa stays crouched by the threshold for a moment, her hands resting on her knees, and lets the coins lie where they are. When she stands, she does it slowly, so Osric can follow every movement.

"Both, Master Osric. I want the case for Maela, and I want to know what is behind your cut, because men who walked out of a quarry on their own feet don't usually leave their hammers lying in the dust." She keeps her voice even. "Tell me one thing first. The men who went to Beregost, did they go willingly? And the one who came back up to your back door, was he sent by the same people who've been pricing your case?"

She does not look toward the corner of the house. Instead she listens, head tilted slightly, for any sound from behind the wall: a scrape, a step on loose chalk, a breath held too long. Nothing comes, and she keeps her eyes on Osric's hands.

Under her breath, to Bram: "Pell's quiet back there. I don't like quiet. Give him a count of twenty before we ask the door anything."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram keeps his shield where it is and lets Osric see he is not reaching for anything.

"I want the case. That's what we were hired for, and it's what Maela will pay for." He looks at the eight gold on the threshold and then at Osric. "Leave the earnest where it lies. If there's a seal on that case, I'll see it before anyone's coin moves."

He turns his head a fraction toward the wall, pitching his voice low.

"Pell. Anybody inside but the warden? Answer me with a word, nothing more."

Then, back to Osric, quieter: "Men in Beregost, drinking on a cut nobody can open. Who hired them to cut it, and who's been asking you about the case? You don't have to say it to me. But if somebody's paying men to make your crew walk off, they'll come asking for the case too, and I'd rather they found me standing in your yard than found you alone with it."

He keeps the shield between Osric and the corner, and waits for the answer from the shadows.

presses.text:
Sefa lets the silence go on a breath longer, watching his hand on the doorframe, and cannot tell what the quiet means. He might be telling the truth. He might simply be a frightened man who has learned to say the same thing twice.

"Boots," she says. "Then bring them out, Master Osric. If one of your men came back for his boots, they'll be by the door, and you can hand them to Bram in the sunlight. That's all anybody needs to see. Nobody has to step past you."

She keeps her hands open and turns her head a fraction toward the wall. "Pell, if you can hear me, say one word. Is the back door open?"

Under her breath, to Bram, without moving her lips much: "I can't read him. He's either telling the truth or he's very well rehearsed, and I can't tell which. Don't take your shield off him yet."

Pell keeps his shoulder to the bend and studies the boot-prints before he looks at anything else. Two sets come back out of the water. The third goes in and never returns.

presses.text:
The wet chalk gives up its story slowly, one print at a time. The two boot-prints that came back out of the water are shallow and rounded at the heel: a man who walked in on his own feet and walked out again, carrying nothing. The third set is different. It goes into the water deep, toes first, the way a man goes when he is being pulled, and the chalk beside it is scored by a heel that scrabbled for a hold and found none. There is no mark coming back. Either it was dragged under, or whoever wore those boots went out another way, through the breach in the far wall.

The pick half-buried in the silt has a fresh chip on its blade. Someone struck stone with it hard, not long ago, and it was not someone working a quarry face.

Beyond the basin, the kneeling man has finished with the vial and is rising, slowly, pulling his hood a little lower. The second man at the crates shifts his weight toward the stair for the first time.

Pell has perhaps two breaths before one of them sees him.

scenes.narration:
Pell keeps his shoulder to the stone and reads the wet chalk at the basin's edge before he reads anything else.

The third set is the one that matters. Pell reads the chalk at the water's lip the way he would read a ledger that someone has tried to smudge: the first two pairs went down to the edge, stood, and came back up, their toes pressed hard and their heels dragging the wet off the shelf. The third went down past the rim, through the shallow water to the foot of the breach, where the fallen stone is heaped. There the prints climb. One boot after another, placed carefully over the loose blocks, and then into the dark of the chamber beyond. No pair comes back over that heap. Nothing has been dragged out through the gap.

"One man went through," Pell breathes. "Alone, and he took his time. The other two went back up the way they came. Nobody's carried back out of there."

He does not step onto the wet shelf. The sunburst on the far wall stays where it is, its rays ending in small flames around the empty hollow, and from this angle Pell can see that the hollow is not blank, only worn, as though something round and heavy sat in it for longer than anyone has been alive. The draught comes out through the breach, cool and dry, and then, as he holds still, it turns: a breath of air drawn the other way, out of the chamber and across the water toward him, carrying a faint smell of cut stone and something that is not quite dust.

Pell counts it. Two came back out. One went in and did not come out by the same road.

messages.text:
Bram does not turn toward the corner. He keeps his shield angled across the gap and counts under his breath, slow, the way he counted sleepers on a long night watch. At ten he hears the seep dripping somewhere under the yard and nothing else. At twenty he lifts his voice, low and flat.

"Pell. Answer me."

He waits one breath, then another, his eyes on Osric's hands and not on the wall.

To Osric, quieter: "Dannic. Took the crew down the track to Beregost. Is he the one who's been paying for the salts, or the one who sold your name to whoever's pricing your case?"

He shifts his weight onto his front foot, ready to move, but keeps the shield between the warden and the back corner.

"Sefa. When I say his name, you get down behind the wheel where Pell was. Don't go round the house. I'll go to the corner myself, if that's what it takes."

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa lets the silence stand, then speaks to Osric, not the wall.

"Then we'll leave the names on your step, Master Osric, since you won't put them on the stone." She straightens, taking care that every movement is slow and visible. "But I'll tell you what I'll do with what I've heard. I'll tell Maela that her warden's crew walked off their own feet, that someone has been bidding up the case, and that you wouldn't say who. She can decide what she wants to pay for that, and whether she wants her name next to yours on any bargain."

She turns her head toward the corner of the house and raises her voice only enough to carry. "Pell. If you're down there, and it's safe, say one word. Is the back door open?"

Then, to Bram, low: "I won't take the case without its seal. But I'd like the eight gold back in my purse before we leave here. Don't argue with me about it."

Pell lets the draught pass over him and draws back one step, out of the line of the basin, until the stone of the bend is between him and the crates. He doesn't turn his back on the water.

Pell eases back past the bend until the stone is between him and the basin, the draught now at his back. The cold light lies on the water without a flicker. For a count of ten nothing moves beyond the breach but the air.

Then the drip under the seep seems to thin, as if something has come between the water and the chalk heap. A voice comes through the gap, low and hoarse and unhurried, a man's. It counts, one to twelve, in the even rhythm a labourer uses for stacking blocks, and it stops at the same word it has stopped at before. Nothing answers it. Cloth drags on stone, and the light on the basin shivers once, as if something above it has shifted its weight.

The count begins again from one.

From the bend Pell sees no one. The breach shows only the heap of fallen chalk, the rays of the sunburst catching the light faintly on the far wall, and the empty hollow at their centre. The voice is not moving closer.

Pell can lean out to the edge of the breach and try to find the man who is counting, or go back up the stair while the cellar keeps its count.

opening.narration:
The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. Pell Dunmore, Bram Halloway and Sefa Marrin have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and somewhere behind them, half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life — a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

screens.text:
The session begins.

The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. You, Pell Dunmore and Sefa Marrin have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and somewhere behind you, half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life, a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

Your records:
Bram Halloway — Human, fighter 5 (Champion; Protection fighting style), former caravan guard of the Trade Way, level 5
HP 44/44 · AC 18 · Speed 30 feet
STR 17 · DEX 12 · CON 15 · INT 10 · WIS 13 · CHA 10
Skills: Athletics +6; Perception +4; Survival +4; Intimidation +3; Tools: land vehicles +3
Saves: Strength saving throw +6 (proficient); Constitution saving throw +5 (proficient); Dexterity saving throw +1; Intelligence saving throw +0; Wisdom saving throw +1; Charisma saving throw +0
Attacks: Longsword +6 to hit, 1d8+3 slashing (1d10+3 two-handed); Javelin +6 to hit, 1d6+3 piercing, range 30/120; Extra Attack: two attacks with the Attack action
Abilities: Proficiency bonus +3; Extra Attack: attacks twice when taking the Attack action; Fighting style, Protection: with a shield, a reaction imposes disadvantage on an attack against a creature within 5 feet of him; Second Wind: a bonus action, regains 1d10+5 hit points; once per short rest; Action Surge: one additional action on his turn; once per short rest; Improved Critical (Champion): a weapon attack crits on 19 or 20; Healer's kit: stabilises a dying creature without a check (ten uses)
Limits: No magic at all; Heavy armour: disadvantage on Stealth; Second Wind and Action Surge return only after a short rest
Counters: Hit dice 5/5; Second wind 1/1; Action surge 1/1; Heroic inspiration 0/1
Money: 23 gp; 14 sp; 30 cp
Worn: Armor / clothing: Chain Mail; Main hand: Longsword; Off hand: Shield
Pack: Bedroll and Hardtack; Healer's Kit; Hempen Rope (50 feet); Javelin ×4; Tinderbox; Torch ×3

Where you are: at the edge of Whitestone quarry yard, facing the slate-roofed house · Time: Day 1 · morning

Pell stays a half-step behind your shoulder, keeping his eyes off the man in the doorway and on the yard: the dropped hammers, the cart only half loaded with its traces slack, the sheds standing open, the untended spoil heaps. In a low voice he says nobody is working this place, that the tools were dropped rather than put away, and that either the crew left in haste or someone made them leave. He tells you to keep your hands in sight, says he wants to see what is behind the man before he judges him, and then steps left to the fallen wagon wheel at the edge of the lower cut, where it gives some cover, and waits.

Sefa, a step ahead, speaks to the man politely. She names Maela Thorn's shop in Beregost, gives her own name and those of her companions, and says you have until sunset to bring the sealed case back. She asks whether the warden is inside. Under her breath she says the place was emptied in a rush, and she wants to know by what before you go near that door.

Osric does not come down the step. He watches your shoulder, then Sefa's hands, then the wagon wheel where Pell has gone to ground, and only then unfolds his arms.

"Maela's," he says. It is not a question. His voice is dry from the dust, and he takes his time with each word.

You read the ground as you would a road you have walked for ten years. The cart's ruts end where the traces were cut loose; the hoofprints head east along the track toward Beregost, deep where a loaded beast was pushed. Two days old, at least, and no one came back for the cart. You say nothing yet, only shift your shield and keep your eyes on the doorway.

"Ninety was Maela's price," Osric says. "Dye-salts, sealed, to her buyer." He turns his head toward the cart, then back. "It's a hundred and sixty now. Gold. On the step, before the lid comes off." He does not smile. "Or the case stays on the shelf, and you walk back down the track with your cart empty."

Behind him, in the dark of the house, something on a shelf catches a little light and then goes dull again. He does not look round at it.

"Crew's gone," he adds, as if it were the same business. "Don't ask me where."

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: The sealed case from Whitestone
+ Quest: The sealed case from Whitestone

Where you are: a few paces into the yard, facing the house doorway · Time: Day 1 · morning

You keep your shield up and hold your ground away from the doorway. You tell Osric in a level voice, loud enough for your companions, that the price agreed with Maela was ninety, payable on delivery. You point out that his cart has stood two days, and ask who has been pressing him for more money. You refuse to pay a hundred and sixty from your own purse and demand to see the case and its seal. You glance once toward the shelf in the dark, and quietly tell Sefa to watch the shelf and to get behind the wheel with Pell if Osric goes for the door.

Sefa, hands open at her sides, also stays back from the step. She says a hundred and sixty is an odd price for salts agreed at ninety, asks whether someone else has been after the case, and asks whether the crew left on their own feet or were made to go. She says she means to take nothing from him. Under her breath she tells you and Pell that Osric is frightened, though not of them, and that the door should be watched.

Osric keeps his eyes on your shoulder and does not say who has been asking. He says ninety was Maela's price, that he set neither figure, and that the hundred and sixty is a matter for the buyer. The crew, he says, walked out of the cut and down the track on their own feet, and nobody made them. The case is in the house, and the seal is seen only when the coin is on the step.

Then his gaze crosses the yard to the wagon wheel, where Pell's cheek is against the iron. He tells him to come out where he can be seen or stay put, since the price is the same either way.

Pell stays where he is. After a while he lifts his head an inch above the rim and tells you and Sefa quietly that two men went out dragging something, and that somebody came back up to the back door after the rest were gone.

Across the yard Osric has not moved his folded arms. His eyes have gone once to the back corner of the house, and then returned to the wheel.

Where you are: in the yard, away from the doorway, facing Osric · Time: Day 1 · morning

You kept your eyes on Osric and spoke to him evenly. You told Pell to stay on the wheel and not come out for him, until you said otherwise. You told Sefa to keep the shelf in her eye and nothing in her hands. You pressed Osric on who dragged something out of the cut, and whether the man at the back door was his crew or someone who needed no key. You told him that you did not care about the hundred and sixty and that you would not stand in his yard all afternoon, and that he should open the door and show the seal or refuse plainly, and Maela Thorn would hear of it either way.

Sefa turned her head slightly toward Pell and asked him quietly who had gone to the back door and whether he had seen the man's face. Then she spoke softly to Osric. She said he had looked at the back corner of his house and not at the case, and that whoever had come up to it frightened him more than you did. She stepped aside out of the line between him and you, her right hand open and her left near the prayer beads at her throat, and offered to stand with him at that door if someone was holding him to his price. Her dagger stayed at her belt. Quietly she told you not to let Osric take the shelf with him if he went for the door.

Pell spoke low to you and Sefa. He said Osric had looked at the back corner twice and did not want you back there. He asked you to keep Osric talking about the ninety and the seal, and said that if he was not back in the time it takes to say "ninety", you were to get Osric into the yard and keep him there. Then he eased onto the top step of the dark stair, shortsword sheathed, and went down.

Osric's jaw worked on nothing for a moment. His eyes went to Sefa's open hands, then to the step under his boots, then once more to the back corner of the house.

"Nobody's holding me to anything," he said. "The price is mine. I set it."

To you, flatter than before, he said the man at the back door was one of his, come back for his boots, and that neither he nor the cut was your business. He came one step down off the threshold, the first time he has moved toward the yard. His hand stays on the ring of keys.

Pell has gone low and fast along the wall of the house into the shadow behind the corner, out of your sight. Osric has now come down the last step and stands at the corner with his keys in his fist, looking at the plank door. He has not yet decided whether to go to it.

Your shield is still up, and Sefa's hands are still open. The question of the coin and the seal has not moved, and Osric has not yet said what he will sell it for. Pell is below. You and Sefa are still in the yard with Osric. What do you do while he decides?

Where you are: the yard of the warden's house, near Osric · Time: Day 1 · morning

Sefa keeps her hands open and her voice low, and she speaks to Osric, not the door. She tells him she believes the price is his, and that the sensible thing is to carry the case out where the light is good and put it on the cart, so you can get a look at the seal. Nobody needs to go through that door to do it.

She waits, watching whether his eyes go to the corner of the house.

Osric's eyes come back from the corner to Sefa's face, and stay there. It costs him something; his jaw sets against it.

He says the case stays in the house until the coin is on the step. Carried out into the sun, he says, it is still the same case, and it does not become Maela's until she pays.

He turns his head toward you, and the keys shift in his fist. The price is a hundred and sixty, in gold. The seal shows when the coin is on the step, and not before, not for you and not for her.

He takes a slow breath, the dust catching in it. There is a letter in with the case, for Maela, he says. She reads that before anybody pays anybody.

Your shield stays where it is, between the warden and the plank door. Osric does not take a step toward the corner. He shifts his weight back onto the threshold, the way a man does when he means to stand where he is, and his free hand comes down flat against the doorframe, not reaching for anything.

Behind him the shelf in the dark gives back its dull glint, and he does not look round at it.

Where you are: yard by the house, between Osric and the plank door · Time: Day 1 · morning

Beside you, Sefa lowered her hands slowly, fingers spread so Osric could see them. She said that a hundred and sixty was more than her purse held, but that she would put all eighteen gold she carried on his step as earnest against Maela's name, and that she would record Maela's pledge on the reverse of the receipt, in her own writing. She asked whether the letter was sealed or open, and offered to read it aloud where you could hear if it was open. When Osric's eyes drifted toward the corner of the house, she spoke his name quietly and waited. Under her breath, to you alone, she said not to let him close the door on the rest of the letter.

You lower your shield the last inch, enough that Osric can see your face over the rim, and you keep the ground between him and the corner. You tell him a letter needs no coin on the step, that he should bring it out for Maela and let you look at the seal on the case. You keep the terms flat: ninety on delivery at Maela's shop, and you carry the case there yourself. Anything the buyer pays above that is for Osric and Maela to settle. Then, more quietly, you tell him he is frightened of that corner and of whoever has been pricing his case, and that you will stand between him and that step as long as he is straight with you. You ask what came out of the cut.

Sefa crouches and sets eight gold pieces and a platinum piece on the threshold stone, bright against the grey chalk. Earnest, she says, against Maela's name.

Osric looks at the coins a long moment and does not reach for them. "Eighteen on my step is eighteen on my step. The price is a hundred and sixty." He shifts his weight back onto the sill. "Leave it where it lies. It doesn't go in my pocket until the rest does."

Sefa asks about the letter. "Sealed. Same wax as the case," he says, his hand flat on the doorframe. "It's for Maela. She reads it first, and you don't." Asked what it says, he is silent so long that the seep drips somewhere under the yard. Then: "It says I'm finished at Whitestone."

You keep your eyes on his face. When his gaze slides once toward the back corner, you don't turn to follow it.

"The cut," you say.

"Stone." His jaw works. "Walls cut before there was a Beregost. A door nobody can open, and water that goes white when it's dark. The men who cut it are in Beregost, drinking on it. Ask them, if you want the rest. Don't ask me."

He comes down one more step off the threshold into the yard and stops, keys in his fist. Behind him the shelf in the dark gives back a dull glint, and he still does not look round at it.

"Stand where you like," he says to you. "Not at my back door. Which of you wants the case, and which of you wants to see what's in my cut?"

Where you are: In Osric's yard, before his open door, between him and the back corner · Time: Day 1 · morning

Sefa stays crouched by the threshold a moment, hands on her knees, leaving the coins where they lie. She rises slowly so Osric can follow every movement. She tells Osric she wants the case for Maela, and also wants to know what lies behind his cut, since quarrymen who left on their own feet seldom abandon their hammers in the dust. She asks whether the men who went to Beregost went willingly, and whether the man who came to his back door was sent by the same people who have been pricing his case. She does not glance toward the corner of the house; she tilts her head, listening for any sound behind the wall, and keeps her eyes on Osric's hands. Nothing comes. Under her breath, to you, she says Pell is too quiet back there, and that you should give it a count of twenty before asking the door anything.

Osric's eyes go to the coins on the threshold and stay there a moment longer than they need to. Then they come back up to Sefa.

"They walked," he says. "Dannic took them down the track to Beregost with their tools on their shoulders. Nobody sent them. Nobody sends a crew anywhere out here." He does not look at the corner of the house. "The one at the back door was mine. Came back for his boots. That's all he was."

Your question he takes more slowly. "Men come up the track asking for salt. Gold, and on the step, not on delivery. Their names aren't on my step, so you don't get them."

Sefa keeps watching his face and his hand on the doorframe, and lets the quiet run. Osric takes the hand from the frame, folds his arms again, and says nothing more about the back door.

"Names aren't on my step," he says to you, and that is the end of it.

Where you are: Osric's yard, shield toward the house corner · Time: Day 1 · morning

Sefa spoke to Osric and told him the names would stay on his step if he wouldn't put them on the stone. She said she would tell Maela that the warden's crew had walked off on their own, that someone had been bidding up the case, and that Osric wouldn't say who. Maela could then decide what that was worth and whether she wanted her name beside his. She called toward the corner for Pell, asking for one word if it was safe, and asking whether the back door was open. Then she told you quietly that she would not accept the case without its seal, yet she wants the eight gold back in her purse before you leave.

Osric's eyes came off the corner when you said the foreman's name, and went to your face and stayed there.

"Dannic walks where I send him," he says. "He took the crew down the track. What he says in Beregost is his own business, and what anyone pays him is not mine to count." He shifts his weight on the sill. "I don't sell my men. I sell salt."

Nothing answers Sefa's call from the stair. The seep drips somewhere under the yard, and the shadow inside the plank door stays a shadow.

Osric's jaw tightens at the call for Pell. His gaze slides once toward the back of the house before he drags it back to Sefa.

"Tell her," he says to her, flat. "Tell Maela the warden's crew walked, and that the price is a hundred and sixty. She can read the rest in the letter." He does not look at the threshold stone, where the eight gold and the platinum piece lie in the sun. "The coin stays where it lies until the rest is on the step. You can argue with Bram about that. I won't."

He settles his folded arms again, and the keys at his belt make a small dry sound against his apron.

Nothing else comes up from the cellar. The yard holds its breath, and the sun has moved a finger's width along the spoil heaps since you started counting.

Where you are: salt yard before the warden's house, shield across the gap, facing Osric · Time: Day 1 · morning

The session is over.

Bram stops at the edge of the yard and lets the others come up on his flanks. He doesn't take his eyes off the doorway.

"Hold here a moment, Pell, Sefa." Quietly, to the two of them: "Pell, go wide to the left, keep behind the spoil heap, and tell me if anything moves up on the terraces. Sefa, stay with me and keep your hands where he can see them."

He sets his shield a little higher and walks forward three slow paces, far enough to be heard across the yard but not so far that he's in the doorway's reach.

"Warden! Maela Thorn, the apothecary in Beregost, sent us. We're for the sealed case of dye-salts, the one that's to go to her shop by sunset." He lifts his empty hand and nods at the half-loaded cart, the scattered tools. "Where's your crew? Nothing's worked here since the bell, by the look of it. Is everyone all right?"

He keeps his longsword in its scabbard, but his eyes go to the ring of keys, then to the shadow inside the house, then back to the man's folded arms, reading whether he is waiting for a greeting or for something else.

Bram keeps his shield up and does not move closer to the doorway. He speaks evenly, loud enough for Pell and Sefa to hear.

"Ninety, Osric. That's what Maela agreed with us, and it's to be paid on delivery, not on the step." He tips his head toward the track behind them. "I've walked this road ten years. Your cart's been standing two days, not since the bell this morning. So you're telling me the crew left two days back, and somebody's been asking you for more money since. Who?"

He lets the question sit, watching Osric's face and the hand that has not left the doorframe.

"I'm not paying a hundred and sixty out of my own purse, and I'm not carrying an argument back to Maela's shop. Show me the case. Let me see the seal. If it's what she bought, she'll pay the ninety in her own shop, and I'll stand for it. If it isn't, we'll all go back and tell her so."

He glances once, quickly, toward the shelf in the dark, then back to Osric.

Quietly, out of the side of his mouth, to Sefa: "Watch the shelf, not his hands. And if he goes for the door, you get behind the wheel with Pell."

Bram doesn't look at the back corner. He keeps his eyes on Osric's face and lets his voice drop a little, flat and patient, the way he'd talk a nervous mule off a bridge.

"Pell, you stay on that wheel. Don't come out for him. But when I say so, I want you round the back corner, slow, and I want to know who went up to that door." He glances at Sefa. "You keep the shelf in your eye. Nothing in your hands."

To Osric: "Two men dragged something out of your cut. Who? Where to? And the one who came back to the back door, was he one of your crew or somebody who didn't need a key?"

He shifts his weight onto his front foot, shield still up, and does not raise his sword.

"I don't care about your hundred and sixty. That's between you and whoever's been asking. But I'm not standing in your yard all afternoon while you decide whether to sell me a case that belongs to Maela's buyer. Open the door, let me see the seal, or tell me plainly you won't, and we'll go back down the track and tell Maela so. Either way, you'll have Maela Thorn to answer to, not us alone."

He waits, counting the breaths.

Bram doesn't follow Osric's eyes to the back corner. He takes two long steps across the yard, placing himself between the old warden and the plank door, shield angled so it covers Osric's line of sight to the corner. He keeps his sword in its scabbard.

"Osric, stay where I can see you. Keys in your hand is fine. Let your other hand be empty."

He keeps his voice low and even, the way he'd talk to a horse on a bad slope.

"Sefa, you're with me. Watch his hands and the shelf. If he moves for that door, you say so, and don't go after him." Then, quieter, without turning his head: "Pell. Whatever you see back there, tell me before you touch it. I want Osric in the yard and I want the case in the yard too, if it's here at all."

Bram looks at the keys in Osric's fist, then back at his face.

"You say the price is yours. Then tell me what you'd sell the case for, to me, and whether you'll show the seal before anyone's coin comes out. I'm listening."

Bram lowers his shield an inch, enough that Osric can see his face, and does not step back from the door.

"A letter for Maela. Then fetch it out and let her read it, and let me see the seal on the case while you're at it. A letter doesn't need a coin on the step."

He looks at the keys in Osric's fist, then at the hand flat against the doorframe.

"Here's my offer, and it's the only one I'm making. Ninety is what Maela agreed, and she pays it on delivery. I'll carry the case to her shop with my own hands. If the hundred and sixty is what your buyer wants, you take that up with Maela, not with three hired people on a road. You'll know by sunset whether she'll pay it, and so will I."

He drops his voice.

"Two men dragged something out of your cut. Somebody came up to your back door after your crew had gone. You're frightened of that corner, Osric, and you're frightened of whoever's been pricing your case for you. I can't stand guard on your house all day. But I'll stand between you and that corner for as long as you're honest with me. What's in that cut?"

Without turning, he calls low over his shoulder toward the wall: "Pell. Talk to me. Is there anybody inside but the warden?"

Bram keeps his shield where it is and lets Osric see he is not reaching for anything.

"I want the case. That's what we were hired for, and it's what Maela will pay for." He looks at the eight gold on the threshold and then at Osric. "Leave the earnest where it lies. If there's a seal on that case, I'll see it before anyone's coin moves."

He turns his head a fraction toward the wall, pitching his voice low.

"Pell. Anybody inside but the warden? Answer me with a word, nothing more."

Then, back to Osric, quieter: "Men in Beregost, drinking on a cut nobody can open. Who hired them to cut it, and who's been asking you about the case? You don't have to say it to me. But if somebody's paying men to make your crew walk off, they'll come asking for the case too, and I'd rather they found me standing in your yard than found you alone with it."

He keeps the shield between Osric and the corner, and waits for the answer from the shadows.

Bram does not turn toward the corner. He keeps his shield angled across the gap and counts under his breath, slow, the way he counted sleepers on a long night watch. At ten he hears the seep dripping somewhere under the yard and nothing else. At twenty he lifts his voice, low and flat.

"Pell. Answer me."

He waits one breath, then another, his eyes on Osric's hands and not on the wall.

To Osric, quieter: "Dannic. Took the crew down the track to Beregost. Is he the one who's been paying for the salts, or the one who sold your name to whoever's pricing your case?"

He shifts his weight onto his front foot, ready to move, but keeps the shield between the warden and the back corner.

"Sefa. When I say his name, you get down behind the wheel where Pell was. Don't go round the house. I'll go to the corner myself, if that's what it takes."

The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. Pell keeps close behind Bram at first and barely glances at the man in the doorway. He tells you to keep your hands where the man can see them, since he wants a look at what is behind him before deciding he is only a warden. Then he moves left to a fallen wagon wheel at the edge of the lower cut, where it offers some cover, and waits.

Bram halts at the edge of the yard and holds you and Pell there. He sends Pell wide to the left behind the spoil heap to watch the terraces, and tells you to stay by him with your hands in view. He walks three slow paces forward, shield raised, sword still sheathed, and calls out to the man in the doorway. He names Maela Thorn, the apothecary in Beregost, as the one who sent you, says you have come for the sealed case of dye-salts that must reach her shop by sunset, and asks where the crew is and whether everyone is all right.

Osric does not come down the step. He watches Bram's shoulder, then your hands, then the wagon wheel where Pell has gone to ground, and only then unfolds his arms.

"Maela's," he says. It is not a question. His voice is dry from the dust, and he takes his time with each word.

Pell, at the wheel, has the yard open before him. Bram studies the ground, and says nothing yet. The mule is gone and so is the crew, and the cart stands with its traces cut loose.

"Ninety was Maela's price," Osric says. "Dye-salts, sealed, to her buyer." He turns his head toward the cart, then back. "It's a hundred and sixty now. Gold. On the step, before the lid comes off." He does not smile. "Or the case stays on the shelf, and you walk back down the track with your cart empty."

Behind him, in the dark of the house, something on a shelf catches a little light and then goes dull again. He does not look round at it.

"Crew's gone," he adds, as if it were the same business. "Don't ask me where."

Sefa stops at the edge of the yard, a step ahead of the others, and lets her eyes go over the scene before she speaks. The abandoned hammers, the half-loaded cart with no mule, the single thread of smoke. Her hand settles on the prayer beads at her throat.

"Good morning to you," she calls, pitching her voice to carry without shouting. "We're from Maela Thorn's shop in Beregost. We've come for the sealed case she arranged with the warden here. My name is Sefa Marrin; these are my companions, Pell and Bram." She lets a small, easy smile reach her face. "Is the warden inside? We have until sunset to get the case back to Beregost, and I'd rather not spend the afternoon standing in the dust."

Under her breath, without turning her head, she says to the others: "Keep your hands where he can see them. Something emptied this place in a hurry, and I'd like to know what before we go near that door."

Sefa keeps her hands loose and open at her sides and does not move closer to the step. She looks at Osric for a long moment, then at the cart with its cut traces, then back at his face.

"A hundred and sixty is a strange price for dye-salts that were agreed at ninety yesterday," she says evenly. "Maela doesn't haggle with her own buyers, and she doesn't send us out at dawn to be cheated at the door. So I'd like to understand what's changed since then. Has someone else been asking for this case?"

She lets her gaze drift past him to the dark doorway, just long enough to mark the shelf and the faint glint on it, then returns to his eyes.

"And the crew. You say they've gone, and you don't know where. Did they leave on their own feet, or did someone make them leave?" Her voice softens, though it does not lose its edge. "I'm not here to take anything from you, Master Osric. Whatever happened in this yard, I'd rather know it before I'm standing in the middle of it."

Under her breath, to Bram and Pell: "He's frightened, and not of us. Watch the door."

Sefa doesn't answer Osric's demand. She turns her head a fraction toward the wheel and keeps her voice low.

"Pell, who went to the back door? Did you see his face, or only his back?"

Then she looks at Osric again, and this time she lets her voice soften.

"Master Osric, you've been standing in that door since before we came up the track, and you haven't once looked at the case. You keep looking at the back corner of your house. Whoever came up to it after your crew left, they frightened you more than we do. I can see that plainly." She takes one slow step to the side, out of the line between him and Bram, so that he has nothing to watch but her open hands. "If someone is holding you to this price, tell me who. I'm not a Guild collector and I'm not a patriar's bailiff. I'm a hired hand with a sunset to meet. If the trouble is at your back door, I would rather stand in it with you than have you stand in it alone."

She does not reach for the dagger at her belt. Her right hand stays open, her left resting near the prayer beads at her throat. Quietly, to Bram, without moving her lips much: "If he goes for that door, don't let him take the shelf with him."

Sefa moves before Osric can settle his mind. She crosses the yard in four unhurried steps and stops at the corner of the house, placing herself between Osric and the plank door, close enough that he has to look at her to see past her.

"Master Osric, I believe you that the price is yours," she says quietly. "So let's do the sensible thing. Bring the case out here, into the light, and set it on the cart where Bram can see the seal. You don't need to open that door to do it, and nobody needs to go through it. Whatever is back there can wait for a minute."

She keeps her hands loose and visible and lets her voice stay low, almost confiding. "You're not refusing Maela. You're trying to be careful with a debt, and that I understand. Give me your word that the case is in the house, and I'll give you mine that we'll make the ninety good in her shop, with a receipt, before the coach leaves. Between the two of us, that should be enough to keep you standing on your own step."

Without looking away from Osric, she says to Bram, pitched just loud enough for him: "Keep him talking about the seal. If he takes one step toward that door, stop him by name."

She makes a Persuasion check to keep Osric in the yard, out of the back door's reach, and talking about the case instead of the price.

Sefa keeps her eyes on Osric's face and lets the question of the seal sit between them.

"Master Osric, you don't have to decide about the door yet. Tell Bram what the case looks like. Is it the cedar box Maela described, with the red wax and her mark? If it is, bring it out and we'll all look at it together, here in the sun, where nobody has to wonder what's behind them."

She does not move toward the corner of the house. She keeps her hands open and watches his eyes, and if they go back to the plank door, she says his name once, quietly.

Sefa lets out a slow breath and lowers her hands an inch, slowly, so he can see every finger.

"A hundred and sixty is more than my purse holds, Master Osric, and I won't pretend otherwise. But I have eighteen gold in coin, and I'll put all of it on your step now, against Maela's name, as earnest. You'll have something in your hand before the rest is settled, and I'll write Maela's promise on the back of the receipt in my own hand."

She nods toward the threshold, not the door. "And the letter. Is it sealed, or is it open for Maela to read? If it's open, let me read it here, aloud, where Bram can hear it. I read a clerk's hand as easily as a healer's, and I'll tell you honestly what it says. If it says what you think, you'll know nobody is cheating you, and you won't have to stand on that step deciding alone."

Her eyes stay on his face. When his gaze flickers toward the corner of the house, she says his name once, quietly, and waits.

Under her breath, to Bram: "Don't let him close that door on the rest of the letter."

Sefa stays crouched by the threshold for a moment, her hands resting on her knees, and lets the coins lie where they are. When she stands, she does it slowly, so Osric can follow every movement.

"Both, Master Osric. I want the case for Maela, and I want to know what is behind your cut, because men who walked out of a quarry on their own feet don't usually leave their hammers lying in the dust." She keeps her voice even. "Tell me one thing first. The men who went to Beregost, did they go willingly? And the one who came back up to your back door, was he sent by the same people who've been pricing your case?"

She does not look toward the corner of the house. Instead she listens, head tilted slightly, for any sound from behind the wall: a scrape, a step on loose chalk, a breath held too long. Nothing comes, and she keeps her eyes on Osric's hands.

Under her breath, to Bram: "Pell's quiet back there. I don't like quiet. Give him a count of twenty before we ask the door anything."

Sefa lets the silence go on a breath longer, watching his hand on the doorframe, and cannot tell what the quiet means. He might be telling the truth. He might simply be a frightened man who has learned to say the same thing twice.

"Boots," she says. "Then bring them out, Master Osric. If one of your men came back for his boots, they'll be by the door, and you can hand them to Bram in the sunlight. That's all anybody needs to see. Nobody has to step past you."

She keeps her hands open and turns her head a fraction toward the wall. "Pell, if you can hear me, say one word. Is the back door open?"

Under her breath, to Bram, without moving her lips much: "I can't read him. He's either telling the truth or he's very well rehearsed, and I can't tell which. Don't take your shield off him yet."

Sefa lets the silence stand, then speaks to Osric, not the wall.

"Then we'll leave the names on your step, Master Osric, since you won't put them on the stone." She straightens, taking care that every movement is slow and visible. "But I'll tell you what I'll do with what I've heard. I'll tell Maela that her warden's crew walked off their own feet, that someone has been bidding up the case, and that you wouldn't say who. She can decide what she wants to pay for that, and whether she wants her name next to yours on any bargain."

She turns her head toward the corner of the house and raises her voice only enough to carry. "Pell. If you're down there, and it's safe, say one word. Is the back door open?"

Then, to Bram, low: "I won't take the case without its seal. But I'd like the eight gold back in my purse before we leave here. Don't argue with me about it."

A few things I'd like to see next time:

- **Pell's silence.** My questions to him went unanswered for several rounds. I understand why, since he was out of sight and had his own plan, but a short line from him on the next turn would help me know where he is.
- **The coins.** Sefa's eight gold is still on the threshold. I'd like to know whether Osric or Bram takes it back, because it matters to Sefa's purse.
- **The Insight failure.** I'm fine with a failed read. It left me uncertain about Osric's story, which suits the scene. I'd just like the next clue about the back-door man to come from somewhere, even if it's a bad one.

Thanks to Bram's player too. His careful positioning gave us room to talk without anyone getting hurt.

The session begins.

The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. You, Bram Halloway and Sefa Marrin have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and somewhere behind you, half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life, a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

Where you are: at the edge of Whitestone quarry yard, facing the slate-roofed house · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram halts at the edge of the yard and holds the other two there. He quietly sends you wide to the left, behind the spoil heap, to watch the terraces for movement. Sefa is to stay beside him. He walks three slow paces forward, shield raised, sword still sheathed, and hails the man in the doorway. He names Maela Thorn, the apothecary in Beregost, as the one who sent you, says you've come for the sealed case of dye-salts due at her shop by sunset, and asks where the crew is and whether everyone is all right. Sefa, a step ahead, speaks too, politely. She gives her name and yours, and says the case must be back in Beregost by sunset, so you'd rather not linger. She asks whether the warden is inside. Under her breath she tells the others to keep their hands in sight and says something emptied this place in a hurry.

You had already gone to ground behind the fallen wagon wheel, to the left, at the edge of the lower cut. The man, Osric, does not come down the step. He watches Bram's shoulder, then Sefa's hands, then the wheel where you are crouched, and only then unfolds his arms.

"Maela's," he says. It is not a question. His voice is dry with dust, and he takes his time over each word.

From the wheel the yard lies open: the lifting frame bare of its rope, the shed doors wide, the spoil heaps with nobody picking through them. Behind the house, where the cut narrows, a line of boot-prints runs down toward the track, and beside it a line of hoofprints that stops and starts. The mule is gone and so is the crew.

"Ninety was Maela's price," Osric says. "Dye-salts, sealed, to her buyer." He turns his head toward the cart, then back. "It's a hundred and sixty now. Gold. On the step, before the lid comes off." He does not smile. "Or the case stays on the shelf, and you walk back down the track with your cart empty."

Behind him, in the dark of the house, something on a shelf catches a little light and goes dull again. He does not look round at it.

"Crew's gone," he adds, as if it were the same business. "Don't ask me where."

Behind you, in the yard, Sefa asked you quietly who had gone to the back door and whether you had seen his face. She then spoke gently to Osric, saying he had watched the back corner of his house rather than the case. She said that whoever came up to it frightened him more than you did, and she offered to stand with him if someone was holding him to his price. She moved a step sideways so she was no longer between him and Bram, her hands open. She told Bram not to let Osric take the shelf with him if he went for that door.

Bram told you to stay on the wheel, then to go round the back corner slowly when he gave the word. He pressed Osric on who had dragged something out of the cut, and told him to open the door and show the seal or refuse plainly, or you would all go back and tell Maela Thorn.

Then you went, and Osric answered in the yard behind you. He said nobody was holding him to anything and that the price was his. Bram heard that the man at the back door was one of Osric's, back for his boots, and that he and the cut were not your business. Osric came one step down off the threshold, his hand on his keys.

You go down the stair one step at a time, weight on the wall side where the treads do not talk. Nine steps of cut chalk, cold as a cellar in winter, and the sound of the yard falls away above you until there is only the drip of seep. At the bottom the passage turns, and a shelf is cut into the wall: linen bundles wrapped in black wool, a few already open, and a shallow dish of pale crystals gone grey at the rim. You do not touch them. Beyond the turn a faint light lies on the wet floor, not lamp-yellow but cold and white, like moonlight on snow in a room with no window.

The scrape comes again from that way, short and deliberate, a stone shifting in water. Then nothing. No footsteps, no breath, only the drip, and the white light trembling on the channel where the seep runs.

Where you are: the chalk passage below the back door · Time: Day 1 · morning

You stop with your back against the cold wall and let the drip fill the silence for a slow count of ten. The scrape does not come again. Whatever is moving down there is either waiting or has been told to.

You breathe a quiet word to Bram and Sefa, though you can't know whether they hear it: the light isn't from a lamp, shouting from below would not mean Osric's men coming up, and they should watch the back door.
