Pell stays a half-step behind Bram's shoulder and does not look at the man in the doorway for long. He looks at the yard instead: the hammers lying in the dust, the half-loaded cart with its traces hanging loose, the open shed doors, the spoil heaps with no one picking through them.

"Nobody's working this place," he says quietly, not moving his lips much. "Tools dropped, not put away. Somebody left in a hurry, or somebody made them leave." He lets his eyes travel back to the house and the man's folded arms. "Keep your hands where he can see them. I want to see what's behind him before I decide he's just a warden."

He takes one step to the left, toward the edge of the lower cut where a fallen wagon wheel gives some cover, and waits to see whether the man moves.

Pell keeps his cheek against the cold iron rim of the wheel and lets his eyes go past Osric to the back of the house, where the cut narrows and the tracks run.

"A hundred and sixty," he says under his breath, loud enough for Bram to hear and no louder. "Maela said ninety, and ninety was already a fair price for walking out here. Ask him what happened to the crew before you ask him for anything. A man who won't say where his mule went is a man who may know where somebody else went too."

He stays low and studies the ground behind the house. The boot-prints run down toward the track, and he wants to know whether they were walked or dragged, and how many went out with their feet dug in.

[Roll the die: Investigation, Intelligence +4 (proficient) → DC 10]

Pell reads the dust the way he reads a ledger: from the bottom line up, looking for where the figures stop agreeing with themselves.

The boot-prints come down out of the cut in a loose line, and most of them are walked, heel-first, the stride long and easy. But three sets, close together near the back corner of the house, dig deep at the toe and skid. Someone was being pulled, or pushed hard, and was not going willingly. Beside those marks the hoofprints stop and start, and one of them has a shoe that is badly set. A mule that was led off in a hurry, not ridden.

He does not say any of it aloud yet. He keeps his voice to Bram and Sefa, low and flat.

"Two of them walked. Three were dragged, and the dragging starts at the back of the house, not the yard." He shifts his weight so the wheel's shadow stays over him. "Osric's still telling us they went on their own feet. Some of them didn't."

He lifts his eyes to the doorway, then past it to the shelf in the dark, where the thing caught the light.

"Bram, don't pay him a copper until you've seen the seal. Sefa, when he says 'the coin on the step,' ask him to show you the wax first, and keep your eyes on the shelf while he does." He pauses. "I'm going round the back of the house. If the tracks go in there, I want to know which door they used before anyone walks through the front."

He begins to move, low and quiet, toward the corner of the house, keeping the cart between himself and the step.
[Roll the die]

The marks give up their story easily once you know how to read them. Three sets of heels, dug in and skidding, run from the back corner of the house to a low plank door in the rear wall, and the door stands a finger's width open on a dark stair. Whoever was dragged went down that way, not out through the yard. A fresh boot-print sits on the top step, turned toward the house, not the track. Someone went back in that door after the others were taken, and it was not a man in a hurry.

The shadow on the lintel is wet, and the wax-smell of a fresh-broken seal hangs faintly in the air by the step. Somebody has been in the back of this house this morning, and they did not leave by the front.

Through the open gap, Pell hears a short scrape from below, then nothing.

Osric's voice carries round the corner from the front. "Have you found what you were looking for, or are you going to stand there till the sun goes down?"

Pell can stay at the back door and listen, slip down the stair in silence, or go back round to the wheel and tell Bram and Sefa what he has found before anyone moves.

[Onward]

Pell does not go down the stair. He crouches on the flagstone beside the open door, back to the wall, and listens. The scrape comes again from below, short and deliberate, like a boot shifting on stone, then nothing.

He lifts two fingers to his lips and gives the low, two-note whistle the Lower City roofs used for *come quiet, something's wrong*. Then he taps the wall twice, so it carries round the corner to where Bram stands.

"Back door's open," he says to the air, pitched for the corner and no further. "Fresh boot on the top step, going in. Somebody came back for something after the crew were taken. I'm not going down until someone's watching the front with me."

He keeps his eyes on the dark gap and his hand on the hilt of his shortsword, not drawing it.

Pell keeps his back to the wall beside the door and turns his head toward the front corner, pitched low for Bram and Sefa.

"Osric's looked at the back corner twice now," he says. "He doesn't want us back here. Bram, keep him talking about the ninety and the seal. Sefa, the shelf. If anything in that house moves toward the door, I want to hear it before I see it."

He glances at the dark gap and the scrape-marked step.

"Whoever came back up didn't come out with the crew. Light boots, and no hurry in them. I'm going down the stair, quiet. If I'm not back in the time it takes you to say 'ninety,' get Osric out into the yard and keep him there."

He does not wait for an answer. He eases a foot onto the top step, shortsword still sheathed, and starts down into the dark.

Pell stops on the top step, weight over the balls of his feet, and waits for the stone to tell him whether it will creak. He pulls his cloak in tight around the studded leather so the buckles don't chime, and listens to the cold air coming up from below before he commits his other foot.

"Going down slow," he breathes to the wall, pitched for Bram's ear only. "If anyone shouts, it's me, and it's not a warning."

He sets his feet down one at a time, keeping to the edges of the steps where the stone is least worn.

[Roll the die]

The stone holds. Pell reaches the foot of the stair without a creak and stops in the mouth of a low cellar, pressed to the cold wall.

A lamp burns on a hook at the far end, turned low. Under it, a quarryman in dust-grey leathers sits against a timber post with his wrists bound behind him and a rag tied across his mouth. His eyes find Pell's shape in the stairwell before anything else moves. He does not make a sound, but his head jerks once toward the far corner.

There a stranger kneels among stacked crates in a dark travelling cloak with the hood up. He has already pried the lid off one crate, and the straw inside is pushed aside. A flat case of pale wood lies open on the floor beside him, its seal broken and its lid thrown back. He is turning something over in his gloved fingers, a small glass vial, holding it up to the lamp to see the colour. He has not looked toward the stair.

Something else lies at the edge of the lamplight: a second case, still sealed, with a seal of red wax and a thumb-print pressed into it. Beside it, on the flagstones, the dust is smeared with the drag of heels.

The stranger murmurs to himself, the words too low to carry, and reaches for the next crate.

Pell can move now, while the man's back is turned, and he has the shortsword and two daggers and the advantage of the stair behind him. He can wait and watch what the stranger does with the vial. He can go to the bound quarryman first and cut him loose. Or he can call up the stairs to Bram and bring the whole yard down into the cellar.
[Onward]

Pell stops with his back to the cold wall and lets the drip fill the silence for a count of ten. The scrape does not come again, so whatever is moving down there is either waiting or has been told to.

He keeps his voice to a breath. "Light's not from a lamp. Bram, Sefa, if you hear shouting from down here, it isn't Osric's men coming up. Watch the back door."

He slides one boot forward along the wall, keeping off the wet channel, and crouches at the bend with his shortsword still sheathed. Before he leans out to look, he sets his hand flat against the stone and tilts his head, listening past the seep for breathing, cloth, or the click of a boot on chalk.

Pell hears it under the drip: a slow breath, drawn and let out through the teeth, the way a man breathes when he is working at something with his hands. Cloth whispers against stone. Two sounds, not one, and the second is lighter, a person standing still.

He leans out a finger's width past the bend. The white light comes from a shallow basin cut into the floor, where the seep pools over something pale that shines like ice. In its glow a dark-cloaked figure kneels with his back half to the passage, sliding a small glass vial into a fold of his sleeve. Beyond him, at the edge of the light, the quarryman's boots are visible on the flagstones, and a second pair stands behind a stacked pile of crates. Those boots do not move. Whoever wears them is watching the stair.

The kneeling man is not hurrying. He glances once at the basin, then closes his gloved hand around a second vial, and murmurs something that sounds like a prayer said backwards.

Pell has the advantage of the bend and the dark. The man at the crates has not seen him. The kneeling man has not turned. Nobody has yet called out.

Where you are: the bend of the chalk passage, under the back door · Time: Day 1 · morning

Pell doesn't trust the silence, but he doesn't waste a breath on it either. He stays low, shortsword sheathed, and eases his head round the bend just far enough to see the basin and the light coming off it. He keeps his hand on the wall and his weight on the balls of his feet, ready to pull back the moment anything turns toward him.

"Water and chalk, no boots," he breathes, pitched for the stair and no further. "Whatever knocked that stone went through the gap ahead. I'm going to look at the light before I walk into it."

He watches the basin's edge and the dark beyond the gap for any sign of a cloak or a hand, and waits for the draught to shift before he moves.

Pell keeps his shoulder to the bend and studies the boot-prints before he looks at anything else. Two sets come back out of the water. The third goes in and never returns.

"Somebody walked into that water and didn't walk out," he breathes, pitched only for the stair. "Or somebody went in on the one foot and got carried. Nothing else here is moving."

His eyes go to the sunburst on the far wall, the rays ending in little flames, the hollow in the middle that is empty. He doesn't know the sign, but he knows the look of a thing that was taken out of its place.

"That hollow's the shape of something that was set in it and then lifted out. The case in the crates is one thing. I want to know what's in that hollow before anyone takes a step past the basin."

He keeps his hand flat on the wall, the vial-thief's glow still lighting the water, and waits for the draught to change.
[Roll the die]

[Onward]

The wet chalk gives up its story slowly, one print at a time. The two boot-prints that came back out of the water are shallow and rounded at the heel: a man who walked in on his own feet and walked out again, carrying nothing. The third set is different. It goes into the water deep, toes first, the way a man goes when he is being pulled, and the chalk beside it is scored by a heel that scrabbled for a hold and found none. There is no mark coming back. Either it was dragged under, or whoever wore those boots went out another way, through the breach in the far wall.

The pick half-buried in the silt has a fresh chip on its blade. Someone struck stone with it hard, not long ago, and it was not someone working a quarry face.

Beyond the basin, the kneeling man has finished with the vial and is rising, slowly, pulling his hood a little lower. The second man at the crates shifts his weight toward the stair for the first time.

Pell has perhaps two breaths before one of them sees him.

Pell lets the draught pass over him and draws back one step, out of the line of the basin, until the stone of the bend is between him and the crates. He doesn't turn his back on the water.

"Two men in here, and the quarryman bound by the lamp," he breathes, loud enough for the stair and no further. "The one that went through the breach didn't come back. Bram, if I'm not up those steps in a minute, the cellar's theirs."

He slips a dagger from his belt and holds it low against his thigh, not raised, and sets his other hand flat on the wall. Then he waits, counting the drip, for the man at the crates to step into the light or the kneeling one to turn around.

I liked that Pell's reading of the ground kept turning up new information. The counting voice in the breach is a strong hook, and I'm curious what's in that empty hollow. I'd be glad to pick it up again next session with Bram and Sefa.

Yes, a few. The one I most wanted to try was cutting the bound quarryman loose while the kneeling man had his back turned. I kept weighing it against going up the stair for Bram and Sefa, and then the scene moved on before I committed. I also wanted Pell to take a closer look at the sunburst on the far wall, since the empty hollow seemed to matter, and I never got him to study it. And I'd have liked to tell Bram and Sefa more clearly what I was planning before I went down the stair, so the back door wasn't left so thin.

The other two were Bram Halloway, the human fighter in chain mail with a shield, and Sefa Marrin, the human warlock who heals with light. Those are the characters from the campaign file, and I took their actions from what the game master told me they did: Bram holding the line and questioning Osric, Sefa speaking gently and watching the shelf.

I don't know who the other two players are, or how they play. I only knew them as the people behind Bram and Sefa. That's why I kept my lines to Pell's own words, pitched so the characters would catch them, and why I was careful not to assume what they had heard or seen.
